translation:
No one like that can be found. In the Kali Yuga many ascetics wearing the garb of renunciation will be found, but true saints of Shri Hari will not be found however much one searches. From atop Kailash, flames are seen rising in all four directions — flames of lust, anger, greed, hypocrisy, and the like. In sacrificial rites (yajnas), the flames of violence are seen blazing. At places of pilgrimage, the flames of craving for charity and offerings are seen. Looking toward Gujarat, however, a little greenness appears that brings peace to the mind — his own devotees are seen waiting eagerly for him. Vaishnav Jivandasji, like the kunj bird that hides its eggs in the sand at the seashore and goes off to graze as far as Lake Mansarovar yet never forgets its young or the way back, set out for Gujarat in that same spirit, to meet the devotees who kept him in remembrance.

In Aryavrat he passed through the region of Shiva's Ekpad Ganas. While making the panchakoshi (five-stage) circumambulation of Kashi, the site for the darshan of the Ekpad Ganas comes midway. Kashi may only be a place that commemorates these Ganas, but Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj actually went to the true, original land of these Ganas and had a direct experience of them there — such was his capability. For the sake of his own devotees he made this journey all the way to the Himalayas of Bharatvarsha (India), for the sake of true devotion. He gained knowledge about every branch and sub-branch of the tradition. Having left his own people at places such as Chanderiya and Ujjain, Jivanji Maharaj now turns back for the welfare of those kinsmen. The longing awakens in him to accomplish the task he had come to do, and so he began the tradition of Uda Dharma and spread pure, unblemished devotion.

When Jivanji Maharaj was preparing to come from Malwa to Gujarat, nine devotees from there also got ready to leave their homeland and come along with him. After they had gone halfway, Jivanji Maharaj felt like testing whether the love of these devotees was genuine. So, saying "I can walk no further now," Jivanji Maharaj sat himself down. The devotees thereupon left their belongings lying right there, seated Jivanji Maharaj in a palanquin, and carried him a distance of five kos (about ten miles). Because they passed Jivanji Maharaj's test, by his own power he had their bundles brought to that very spot; and once the bundles arrived, he had rice and other provisions taken out from them and ordered a meal to be prepared. These loving devotees had not become so infatuated as to be unwilling to accompany Jivanji Maharaj — rather, Jivanji Maharaj himself had said:

_Pendama pad Jivana | jahan nikse harike das ||_
_Sang rahe ke le chale | pure mankee aas ||1||_
("Take your stand on the path, Jivan, wherever the servants of Hari pass by. Either they will stay with you, or they will take you along — either way your heart's longing will be fulfilled.")

If we wait patiently upon the very path along which God's devotees are known to pass, holding fast to that spot, then someday, whenever a true saint happens to come that way, he will either remain with you and remove all the desires of your mind and the sufferings of the disease of worldly existence, or he will take you along with him. Such feelings were firmly fixed in the minds of these devotees. That is why true Sadgurus would take such people along with them. Whoever passes through the guru's test may attain their welfare, but this test must be endured — and so Kabir says:

_Kabir khari kasoti Ramki | khota take na koy ||_
_Ram kasoti te sahe | je jivat mratak hoy ||2||_
("Kabir says: the true test is Ram's own test — no false one can withstand it. Only one who is dead while yet alive can endure the test of Ram.")

When a true examination is made of who is genuine and who is a mere hypocrite in the practice of devotion to Ram, those who are weak, soft, and hypocritical fail it. So the true test of devotion to Ram can be borne only by those devotees who, having given up their own ego, worship him free of desire.

These devotees passed the test of Ram. Those devotees who were prepared to follow the Uda Dharma tradition that Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj set going had to face a situation as hard as, or even harder than, that of the devotees from Malwa. Because Jivanji Maharaj made them give up the company of their own kinsfolk, it is hard even to imagine today how difficult it must have been for those who accepted this faith to observe the prohibition against eating with their own kin, parents, or relatives, and against giving and taking daughters in marriage outside the fold. Moreover, they had to boycott the Vedic path of ritual observance, keep strict abstinence from all vices, wholly reject the degrading custom of sutak (birth/death ritual pollution) and the taboo of menstrual impurity, and put a complete stop to practices such as beating the chest in mourning (chhajiya) and the buying and selling of brides and grooms — one has only to consider how much hardship this must have caused in everyday worldly dealings. For us, in our present circumstances, thanks to the merit and grace of our forefathers and elders, we face not the slightest difficulty in observing these customs. Before any new practice can be established, it is always very hard to clear away the old rubbish. Thus our whole community of devotees today does not have to undergo even a trace of the testing of worldly custom and Vedic ritual that they went through. To that extent we are fortunate indeed. Blessed is such a Sadguru, and blessed are such brave and valiant devotees.
